name: Filling the gap for untagged fonts: copy weighted Google tags from nearest tagged neighbours (traits or embeddings), versus a short human tagging pass in Google's vocabulary
what_it_is: Two ways to give the families that lack Google's mood labels the same weighted labels Google gives its own fonts. (A) Tag transfer: for each untagged font, average the Google Expressive/Theme weights (0-100) of its k nearest tagged fonts, where 'nearest' comes from measured shape traits or a font-image embedding, or fit a regression from traits to weights. Output: one file, family -> {tag: weight}. (B) Human pass: a person looks at a rendered specimen of each untagged font (name hidden) and ticks tags from Google's vocabulary (20 'Expressive' moods such as Active, Loud, Calm, Futuristic, Playful; about 13 'Theme' tags such as Techno, Pixel, Brush, Stencil). Output: the same file with labels at full strength. Hybrids are possible (transfer or an LLM pre-fills, the person confirms), but this item compares the two pure routes.
provider_and_url: Labels to imitate: Google Fonts tags, https://github.com/google/fonts/tree/main/tags (tags/all/README.md calls families.csv 'expressive and typographic tags, human assessed' and quant.csv 'measured values, machine assessed'; Google staff still edit it, last commit seen 2026-09-23). Precedents: O'Donovan, Libeks, Agarwala, Hertzmann, 'Exploratory Font Selection Using Crowdsourced Attributes', ACM TOG 33(4) 2014, https://www.dgp.toronto.edu/~donovan/font/ ; Kulahcioglu and de Melo, 'FontLex', LREC 2018, https://aclanthology.org/L18-1010/ and 'Predicting Semantic Signatures of Fonts', IEEE ICSC 2018, http://gerard.demelo.org/papers/font-attributes.pdf ; Kitajima, Haraguchi, Uchida, 'Font Impression Estimation in the Wild', ICDAR 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.15236 ; Chen, Wang, Xu, Jin, Luo, 'Large-scale Tag-based Font Retrieval with Generative Feature Learning', ICCV 2019, https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.02072 .
catalog_coverage: Counted by me (merged catalog rebuilt with the app's own mergeSources: 2,099 rows = Google 1,760, Fontshare 64, Velvetyne 63, Collletttivo 26, Tunera 23, Use & Modify 163; scripts in docs/research/font-vibe-search/results/evidence/). Google: 1,523 families have a full Expressive mood vector in tags/all/families.csv; 88 more have mood rows only at single axis positions (variable fonts, e.g. wght@100/400/900), which the app's parseGoogleTags skips on purpose (server/catalog.ts), so they show few or no tags; 149 have no mood row anywhere (they collapse to about 74 designs: Fusion Pixel 27 variants, Redaction/Redacted 9, DSEG 11, Big Shoulders 6, Iosevka 5, Monaspace 5, DejaVu 4...). In the app today 137 Google rows have zero tags and 376 have only 1-2. Non-Google: none of the 339 families (Velvetyne 63, Collletttivo 26, Tunera 23, Use & Modify 163, Fontshare 64) has any Google-vocabulary mood tag. They carry the foundries' own words (pixel, wonky, damage, mechanistic) or Fontshare's use cases (Magazines, Books, Posters). So the real gap is 339 + 149 = 488 families (23% of the catalog), about 327 distinct designs (253 first-word groups among the 339, plus 74 among the Google 149); the '~340' in the brief is only the non-Google part. Both routes can cover all 488; the human pass covers whatever subset the person chooses.
granularity: Per family. Google's labels are per family; variable fonts also have per-axis-position rows that differ (Archivo has Loud 75 only at wght 900). Italic and weight are not labelled separately, so either route copies one label set to every style.
signal_type: Semantic mood in Google's vocabulary, inferred from geometric shape or overall visual look via neighbours (transfer), or read off the rendered look by a person (human pass).
mood_dimensions_covered: Measured by me (evidence/transfer_loo.py): hide one tagged Google family at a time (1,523 families with Expressive vectors), predict its 0-100 weights from its 15 nearest other families, score per tag with AUC and precision@20 for 'weight >= 60'. Features: Google category, Google stroke class, Google's stroke-width measurements (quant.csv), legacy 1-10 thickness/slant/width (only 706 families have these), plus TF-IDF of the DESCRIPTION text. Neighbours sharing a first name word (Big Shoulders, Fusion Pixel...) were excluded to avoid sibling leakage. Best mix (metadata + text, no siblings): Active AUC 0.89 / P@20 0.30 (base rate 5%); Loud 0.93 / 0.80; Calm 0.90 / 0.75; Futuristic 0.80 / 0.30; Techno 0.76 / 0.10; Playful 0.85 / 0.60; Sophisticated 0.94 / 0.45; Fancy 0.94 / 0.55; Rugged 0.77 / 0.30; Vintage 0.81 / 1.00; Pixel 0.88 / 0.75; Brush 0.78 / 0.10; Stiff 0.79 / 0.10; Innovative 0.89 / 0.10; Happy 0.84 / 0.15; Cute 0.83 / 0.20; Distressed 0.73 / 0.05; Awkward 0.86 / 0.45. Averages over 26 tags: category-only baseline AUC 0.758 and P@20 0.13; metadata kNN 0.828 / 0.36; text kNN 0.735 / 0.41; metadata+text 0.844 / 0.44 (siblings allowed: 0.875 / 0.55). Reading: heavy-weight or silhouette-driven moods (Loud, Calm, Pixel, Vintage) transfer; fine semantic moods (Techno, Brush, Stiff, Innovative, Futuristic) do not. Motion/active: AUC is fine (0.89) but only 6 of the top 20 are right, and Google's own 'Active' means lively script and comic display (top Active: Faster One 94, Aguafina Script 93, Story Script 91, Arizonia 90, Kaushan Script 89), not speed; corr(Active, Futuristic) = -0.01 across 1,611 families. Foundry words as a free partial map (hand-made strict mapping, evidence/foundry_map.py): 121 of 339 non-Google families (36%) carry at least one word that maps to a Google mood (Vintage 66, Techno 27, Elegant 23, Playful 14, Loud 12, Futuristic 8, Active 7, Calm 7), so foundry text alone cannot supply 'fast/action' for the other 64%. Human pass: covers any mood the person decides on; in Google's vocabulary it inherits the Active-means-lively mismatch, so a custom 'Fast / motion' chip is worth adding.
query_style_specificity: Transfer helps for loose, silhouette-driven requests ('bold', 'calm', 'retro', 'pixel': P@20 0.75-1.00) and fails for tight semantic ones ('techno', 'brush', 'stiff', 'innovative': P@20 about 0.10; 'fast' about 0.30). Kulahcioglu and de Melo find the same pattern: 'technical' is the least predictable of 37 attributes (mean abs error 0.111 on a 0-1 scale) while 'fresh' and 'gentle' are the easiest (0.051). A human pass has no such split: it is as good for 'fast' as for 'calm', provided the person has a chip for it.
quality_evidence: My own held-out test (above) is the main evidence; it is an upper bound for the indie fonts, because the legacy Google metrics (thickness/slant/width) and description text used there do not exist for them; indie fonts have only category, weights and the app's fontkit facts (cap/x-height, features) today. Accuracy did not fall for fonts whose nearest neighbour is far (meta kNN AUC 0.807 outer third, 0.855 middle, 0.819 inner third), so I found no sign of a cliff for unusual fonts, but the test cannot see indie-specific shapes. As a pre-fill for a person it is weak: the top 3 suggested moods per font are truly >= 60 only 29% of the time (>= 40: 43%) against 9% / 16% for random picks, and 24% / 34% for category alone. Literature: O'Donovan 2014 crowd-labelled 200 fonts (31 relative attributes plus 6 binary; 198,400 answers from 639 MTurk workers at $0.07 per task) and predicted 1,278 fonts from glyph-geometry features with gradient-boosted trees; leave-one-out mean absolute error 8.51 on a 0-100 scale (LASSO 10.76). Kulahcioglu and de Melo 2018 extended the 200 to 1,883 fonts with weighted k-NN (k=4) on a CNN embedding of rendered letters: error 0.05-0.11 per attribute (0-1 scale), error rises with distance to the neighbours, and far-away fonts are pulled toward the middle of each scale. Kitajima 2024 (4,000 fonts, 84 tags, about 4 tags per font): ensembling the tags of similar exemplar fonts reached macro F1 0.2913 (precision 0.287, recall 0.351) against 0.2001 for the best plain multi-label CNN, on word images 'in the wild'. Chen 2019 (18,815 MyFonts fonts, 1,824 tags): best retrieval mAP 28.1 / nDCG 70.0 on the 300 most common tags, 18.0 / 44.0 on all 1,684 tags, 16.7 / 37.6 on multi-tag queries. Even with 18k training fonts and deep features, predicted tags are only moderately precise. Google itself fills gaps by hand: tags/all/lowtags.py lists families with fewer than the median number of tags, and its README says the tags are 'human assessed'. [uncertain]
known_noise: Google's labels are noisy themselves: O'Donovan's raters agree on only 69.6% of pairwise answers on average (thin 93.2%, sharp 62.0%), majority votes average 74%, and professional designers' font choices beat MTurk choices only 53% of the time. Positive/unlabeled problem: Kitajima notes that a missing tag does not mean the impression is absent (very thick fonts are often not tagged 'heavy'). Seasonal tags are junk for mood (Kaushan Script Hanukkah 92, Bungee Hanukkah 94); the app already drops them. Exo 2, Saira and Teko have no Active tag at any axis position. Transfer adds its own noise: top-3 moods right 29% (>= 60); regression toward the middle, so extremes are under-expressed. A human pass has self-inconsistency instead; nobody has measured Wouter's, so re-tagging 30 fonts a week later would.
name_and_memory_bias: Transfer and the human pass use letters, not names, so they add little name bias; the person should tag with the name hidden and one neutral specimen text (the outline's Stroop-effect point; unverified by me). The search itself still leans on names and memory. Crude name test (keyword lexicon, evidence/name_bias.py): 72% of the 43 Google Pixel fonts have a literal pixel-type word in the family name, but only 14% of Futuristic, 20% of Techno and 8% of Active positives do, so names rescue literal themes and not moods. Live test (Haiku 4.5, Google tags hidden from all 1,760 Google rows): precision against Google's own tags fell from 57.5% to 40% over four literal/mood queries; Sonnet 5.5 fell from 68% to 53%. Small samples (20-40 picks per cell). [uncertain]
untagged_rows: Measured and bad: rows whose tags are missing are silently pushed down. With Google tags hidden from the 1,760 Google rows (a stand-in for untagged rows) and the foundry rows still tagged, Haiku 4.5 picked 5.2 Google fonts per run instead of 12.2 for 'fast movement or action' (4 and 6 runs), and none at all for 'loud, shouting, impossible to ignore' (0 of 21 picks); Sonnet 5.5 at low effort was much less affected (8.4 vs 9.0). In today's catalog the 137 Google rows with zero tags and the 339 rows without Google moods are in that position. A filled-in row competes fairly only if it reads like a tagged row. Transfer helps but regresses to the middle, so transferred rows still lose on extreme moods; a human pass gives full-strength labels.
text_interference_risk: Not a visual method unless embeddings are used for the neighbours (then render a neutral specimen, never the font name). For the human pass the risk is the person's own: hide the family name and use one fixed sample string.
integration_path: Precomputed data file plus a catalog field. Add server/data/mood-tags.json: {"version":1,"fonts":{"Family Name":{"src":"human|transfer|mapped|google","at":"2026-10-03","w":{"Active":80,"Loud":55}}}} (weights 0-100, Google's tag names, so one vocabulary). In server/catalog.ts: (1) first, free fix: when a Google family has no flat Expressive rows, use its wght@400 row (else the mean over axis rows) instead of dropping them (+88 families, about an hour); (2) merge mood-tags.json into FontEntry.tags before mergeSources, after Google's own tags, keeping 'src' so evaluation can exclude human-tagged rows from silver labels. In server/vibe.ts compactCatalog nothing else changes: the label strings appear in the same 'tags' column. For the search to treat transferred rows fairly add a score step (see search-design): weight 'src' human = 1.0, google = 1.0, transfer = shrunk toward the mean.
tokens_per_row: Measured: Google tags already cost about 14 tokens per Google row (73,203 of 166,277 prompt characters = 25.2k of the 57k Haiku tokens). A 3-5 word human tag set for 339 rows adds about 4k tokens (+7%). Adding two-digit weights to six tags on every Google row would add about 10.8k tokens (+19%). The text is static, so the prompt stays cacheable; any change rewrites the cache once (57k tokens on Haiku, 77k on Sonnet 5.5 / Opus 5; 1-hour cache lifetime measured on this Max login).
vocabulary_alignment: Both routes map onto Google's vocabulary by construction. The foundries' own words (pixel, wonky, damage, mechanistic, curveless) stay as extra terms; 121 of 339 non-Google rows can borrow a Google mood from them. Caveat: Google's 'Active' is lively/playful, not 'fast', so a motion chip is a new term and Google rows will not have it.
explainability: Transfer: yes, by neighbours ('matched because its 5 nearest tagged fonts, named, are Active 70+'), though the shown value is a regressed average. Human pass: yes, a stored label with date and source. Both beat a bare LLM impression.
determinism: Fully deterministic once the file is written (same request, same rows), unlike the live LLM step, whose identical-prompt runs overlapped only 19% (Haiku) to 50% (Sonnet 5.5 low) in my replicate runs.
build_effort: Axis-row fix: about an hour. Human pass: a small tagging page in the app (specimen with name hidden, one chip per Google mood and theme tag, optional LLM or kNN pre-fill, writes mood-tags.json) is about half a day for an agent, plus 2-3 hours of Wouter's time. Transfer: 1-2 days: download about 1,760 Google woff2 from jsDelivr, measure stroke width, contrast, slant, width and weight uniformly for Google and indie files (the app's fontkit facts give only cap/x-height, ascender, features), then kNN and held-out evaluation; embeddings add a rendering + model step (see image-embeddings item).
per_search_cost_and_latency: None per search: both routes are precomputed. Cost is the extra prompt tokens per row (above) and the one cache rewrite when the file changes.
one_off_cost: Transfer: about 1,760 font downloads and some CPU, no API dollars. Human pass: no compute. Optional LLM pre-fill for 488 families would be one batch of roughly 100-150 Haiku calls on the subscription (not run by me).
human_effort: Counted from the catalog: 339 families x 30 s = 2.8 h; grouped by design family (253 first-word groups such as 0xA000 x7, Ductus x6, DOF x7) 253 x 30 s = 2.1 h; adding the 74 untagged Google design groups gives 327 groups = 2.7 h. At 15 s with pre-filled chips 1.4 h; at 60 s 5.4 h. As the catalog grows: a new indie release costs about 30 s at ingestion; Google adds and tags its own fonts. The 30 s per font is the caller's assumption, not something I could measure. Re-tagging a random 30 a week later (about 15 min) would measure the person's own consistency. [uncertain]
asset_access: Google tags: raw.githubusercontent.com/google/fonts/main/tags/all/families.csv, 1.36 MB, already in the session scratch folder (reuse, do not re-fetch). Font files for transfer: Fontsource files on cdn.jsdelivr.net, Fontshare on cdn.fontshare.com, indie files already cached in server/.cache/fonts (578 entries). Velvetyne files come through the app's proxy to GitLab, never velvetyne.fr.
licence_and_provenance: Google tag files: no licence text found in tags/, and the google/fonts repository reports no top-level licence; the Developer API docs page is CC BY 4.0 but that covers the page, not the data [uncertain: the outline's 'CC BY 4.0 for API data' is unverified]. O'Donovan's attribute.zip and Kulahcioglu's signatures are academic releases with no licence found on their pages [uncertain]. A human pass produces Wouter's own labels (no licence issue). Derived numeric labels are not font software, so OFL vs ITF Free Font License matters only if images are rendered (embedding route): OFL allows it; the ITF licence terms for Use & Modify/Velvetyne fonts were not checked by me. [uncertain]
etiquette: One fetch of the tag CSV is enough. If downloading about 1,760 woff2 files from jsDelivr for traits, keep to a few concurrent requests and cache them. Never request velvetyne.fr.
maintenance_and_freshness: Google edits tags continuously (families.csv commits on 2026-09-04 and 2026-09-23 by Google staff), so a transfer model must be re-run on each refresh and its predictions must never overwrite a Google or human label (hence the 'src' field). Human labels are one-off per font. Freeze a dated copy of the Google CSV for any evaluation.
risks_and_limitations: 1) My transfer numbers come from Google-vs-Google fonts; indie fonts have different shapes (display 35% vs 27%, monospace 12% vs 4%; Velvetyne is 59% display) and lack the metadata I used, so real accuracy is lower, probably clearly lower for Techno/Futuristic/Active. 2) Transferred tags are regressed to the middle, so untagged rows still rank lower on extreme moods. 3) Copying Google's vocabulary copies its meaning: 'Active' is not 'fast'. 4) Labels carry the labeller's taste; that is fine for a personal tool but means silver-label evaluation must exclude human-tagged rows. 5) 30 s per font is optimistic if the person has to think; 60 s doubles the cost. 6) Hand-mapping foundry words is a judgement call (my strict map: 121 of 339).
evaluation_hook: Hide-and-recover on Google fonts (done once above): hide a seeded 20% fold (about 350 families, the size of the real gap), predict, compute AUC and P@20 per tag. For the human pass: re-tag 30 random fonts after a week and report agreement. For both: run the same 25 mood and motion requests with and without the new labels and have the person pick the better grid, blind (see evaluation item).
recommendation_for_font_explorer: Use the human pass as the main route, keep transfer as a fallback and an audit, and do two free things first. Why: transfer only recovers the easy moods (Loud, Calm, Pixel, Vintage) and is weakest on exactly the requests that motivated this work (Techno P@20 0.10, Futuristic and Active 0.30), its top-3 suggestions are right 29% of the time, and for indie fonts it runs without the metadata that gave my best numbers. The human pass costs about 2.1-2.8 hours once, is exact in Google's vocabulary, and fixes the measured silent push-down. Smallest first steps, in order: (1) re-parse Google's axis rows (+88 Google families, no human time); (2) map the foundries' own words onto Google moods where unambiguous (121 of 339 get at least one; mark src=mapped); (3) build the small tagging page and tag 30 random indie design groups (about 15 minutes), then rerun 'fast movement or action' twice and check whether the newly tagged fonts rise; (4) if that works, tag the rest, display and sans rows first (about 207 of the 339), and add one custom 'Fast / motion' chip because Google's Active does not mean speed. Relative to the other items: it is the highest-trust label source for the gap; vision labels or image embeddings (other items) are cheaper pre-fillers but my measurement says neighbour-based suggestions are too weak to skip the person; designer descriptions help a little (text kNN AUC 0.735 without siblings). Use transfer afterwards to flag human labels that disagree strongly with their neighbours, and for new fonts until someone tags them.
